chief_complaint: crushing retrosternal chest pain with diaphoresis
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with crushing retrosternal chest pain with diaphoresis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the crushing pain is just severe acid reflux from late-night takeout or a torn muscle from lifting heavy weights at the gym.
concerns: He is worried that he is having a sudden heart collapse like his father did in his early forties.
expectations: He hopes to get strong antacids and pain medicine so he can get back on his feet and go to work tomorrow.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of STEMI (Heart Attack) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate STAT ECG, aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor such as ticagrelor, and Cath Lab activation for STEMI (Heart Attack), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out STEMI (Heart Attack).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Aortic dissection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Radiation with diaphoresis.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

history.answer: Doctor, I have this terrible crushing pain in the center of my chest, and I broke out in a cold sweat about an hour ago.
It started abruptly about an hour ago while I was sitting quietly at my desk at work, and it has been steadily worsening.
It is right behind my breastbone in the middle of my chest, and it feels broad rather than something I can point to with a finger.
It feels like a heavy elephant is sitting on my chest, squeezing and crushing me.
Yes, the tightness radiates down along the inside of my left arm and up into my jaw.
It has been constant and unrelenting for the entire hour without letting up at all.
Right now it is an 8 out of 10, and the pressure feels like it is building.
It started while I was resting, and resting has not made it any better.
No, taking a deep breath, coughing, or changing my posture does not change the pain at all.
No, it is not related to eating, and I haven't had acid reflux, heartburn, or pain when swallowing.
Yes, I am drenched in cold sweat, feeling nauseous, extremely tired, and a bit short of breath.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, cough, or sputum.
No, I haven't had a cold, flu, sore throat, or recent infection.
No, neither leg is swollen or sore, and I haven't been on any long flights or had surgery.
No, there is no rash, redness, or blisters on my chest.
I feel terrified and have an overwhelming sense that something awful is happening to me.
I don't have diagnosed high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, but I haven't had a checkup in a few years.
No, I have never experienced anything like this before, and I've never had any heart tests or procedures.
No, I haven't had any chest injury, and I haven't done any heavy lifting or strenuous workouts.
I thought it was just really bad heartburn from late-night takeout, or maybe I tore a muscle lifting at the gym.
My father collapsed suddenly from chest trouble at forty, so I am terrified the exact same thing is happening to me.
I just want some strong medicine to settle my chest so I can get back home and go to work in the morning.
I don't have any chronic illnesses or ongoing medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never stayed in a hospital.
I don't take any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or health supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any vaping products.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers on occasion.
I work as an office employee in IT and live with my wife in an apartment.
My father had high blood pressure, but no one in my family had a heart attack at an early age.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 130/80 mmHg in both arms, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C.
Patient appears in acute distress, pale, clutching his chest, and visibly diaphoretic.
Normal jugular venous pulsation without distension; estimated central venous pressure is within normal limits.
Chest wall shows no visible lesions, rashes, or deformities; palpation over the sternum, ribs, and costochondral junctions does not elicit tenderness or reproduce the chest pain.
Normal resonance to percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Bilateral vesicular breath sounds are clear to auscultation without crackles, wheezing, or pleural friction rubs.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no third or fourth heart sounds, murmurs, or pericardial friction rub.
Radial, brachial, femoral, and pedal pulses are symmetric, strong, and equal bilaterally with no pulse deficit.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender to light and deep palpation across all quadrants including epigastrium, without guarding or organomegaly.
No pitting edema noted in either lower extremity.
Both calves are supple, symmetric, and non-tender without swelling, warmth, or cords.
